proposedTopics.title: Lending Protocols
proposedTopics.description: Overcollateralized on-chain money markets: suppliers earn interest, borrowers post collateral and draw debt, and a health-factor plus liquidation mechanism keeps the system solvent. Aave V3 and Compound V3 are the reference designs.

proposedTopics.title: Stablecoins
proposedTopics.description: Assets engineered to hold a peg: overcollateralized CDPs (DAI/USDS), algorithmic/seigniorage designs (and why they fail), and the mechanics of minting, burning, and liquidating against a price feed.

proposedTopics.title: Staking, LSTs & Restaking
proposedTopics.description: Turning staked ETH into a liquid, composable asset: Lido's rebasing stETH and wrapped wstETH, and EigenLayer's restaking that reuses that stake to secure additional services for extra yield and extra slashing risk.

proposedTopics.title: Perpetual Futures
proposedTopics.description: Leveraged derivatives with no expiry, kept near spot by a funding rate exchanged between longs and shorts. Covers mark vs index price, funding, and the GMX pooled-liquidity and Hyperliquid orderbook models.

proposedTopics.title: Yield Vaults (ERC-4626)
proposedTopics.description: The tokenized-vault standard that turned yield strategies into composable share tokens: deposit an asset, mint shares whose price grows as yield accrues, redeem for more of the asset — with the rounding and inflation-defense rules that make it safe.

proposedTopics.title: Flash Loans
proposedTopics.description: Uncollateralized loans that are safe because they are atomic: borrow, act, and repay plus a fee within a single transaction, or the whole thing reverts. The primitive behind arbitrage, liquidations, collateral swaps — and many exploits.

proposedTopics.title: Aave V3 aTokens & interest accrual
proposedTopics.description: Supplying an asset to Aave mints an aToken (e.g. aUSDC) that represents supplied principal plus accrued interest: balanceOf is a scaled balance multiplied by the reserve's normalized-income index. Variable debt uses the same scaled-balance pattern with a variable-borrow index, and rates respond to utilization. aTokens remain transferable receipts, but integer ray math means mint, burn, and transfer paths must preserve the scaled accounting.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in defi/lending/ScaledToken.sol implement a scaled-balance token whose balanceOf = scaledBalance * index / RAY and an index that grows with a per-second rate; test/defi/ScaledToken.t.sol. Done when: two suppliers who deposit at different indices each redeem principal + their correct share of accrued interest, and balanceOf increases with time without any transfer.

requirements.purpose: Trace the exact protocol-favorable rounding used to convert between aToken assets and scaled balances

proposedTopics.title: Health factor & liquidation
proposedTopics.description: Aave gates solvency with the health factor: HF = sum(collateral_i * liquidationThreshold_i) / totalDebt, all in a common base currency. Borrow capacity uses max LTV, while liquidation eligibility uses the higher liquidation threshold: HF below 1 permits liquidation. A liquidator repays an allowed portion of debt and receives corresponding collateral plus a configured liquidation bonus; current V3 close-factor behavior depends on health and dust conditions.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in defi/lending/HealthFactor.sol implement computeHealthFactor over multiple collaterals/debts using per-asset liquidation thresholds and a price oracle, plus a liquidate() paying a bonus; test/defi/HealthFactor.t.sol. Done when: a position with HF >= 1 cannot be liquidated, an oracle price drop pushes HF < 1 and enables liquidation, and the liquidator receives collateral + bonus.

requirements.purpose: Derive health factor from weighted liquidation thresholds and distinguish liquidation eligibility from borrowing capacity

proposedTopics.title: Aave e-mode & isolation mode
proposedTopics.description: Aave V3 e-mode applies category-specific LTV, liquidation, and borrowing permissions. V3.7 adds an isolated flag to e-mode categories: only listed category collateral contributes borrowing power, users with other collateral enabled cannot enter, and users inside cannot enable outside collateral. V3.7 removes the legacy isolated-collateral mode that used one collateral, approved debt assets, and a debt ceiling; rollout remains market-specific.

Done when: category collateral receives its configured borrowing parameters, isolated e-mode rejects entry with outside collateral enabled, outside collateral contributes zero borrowing power, and a user inside cannot enable it as collateral.

proposedTopics.title: Compound V3 (Comet)
proposedTopics.description: Compound III (Comet) has one borrowable base asset per deployment: a positive base balance earns supply interest and a negative base balance represents debt. Other supported assets are collateral only—they increase borrowing capacity, do not earn protocol interest, and cannot themselves be borrowed from that deployment. Each market therefore has a single base asset and a curated collateral set.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in defi/lending/Comet.sol implement a single-base-asset market where collateral assets back a base-asset borrow but earn nothing and are non-borrowable; test/defi/Comet.t.sol. Done when: a user can borrow only the base asset, collateral supplied earns no interest, and attempting to borrow a collateral asset reverts.

proposedTopics.title: Overcollateralized CDP stablecoin
proposedTopics.description: A collateralized debt position mints a stablecoin against collateral worth more than its debt: with a 150% minimum collateralization ratio, debt cannot exceed two-thirds of collateral value. Burning stablecoin reduces debt and permits collateral withdrawal subject to safety checks. In Maker's design, collateral-specific rates accumulate stability fees and price data determines the safe debt limit; market arbitrage and protocol conversion facilities support the peg.

proposedTopics.title: CDP liquidation & collateral ratio
proposedTopics.description: The collateralization ratio = collateralValue / debtValue. Below the collateral type's liquidation ratio, the position is unsafe and can be seized for liquidation. Maker's Liquidation 2.0 sells seized collateral in an auction to raise debt plus stability fees and a liquidation penalty, rather than paying a fixed bonus directly. Since oracle-derived collateral value controls eligibility, stale or manipulated pricing can trigger wrongful liquidation or conceal insolvency.

proposedTopics.title: Algorithmic stablecoins & the UST collapse
proposedTopics.description: Terra Classic's market module implemented native stablecoin/Luna swaps by burning the offered coin and minting the requested coin at oracle exchange rates. That makes redemption capacity reflexive: absorbing stablecoin exits expands Luna supply, so falling demand and price can require still more issuance. After the May 2022 collapse, the original chain was renamed Terra Classic and market-module mint/burn swaps were disabled; the new Terra chain launched without native stablecoins or the market module.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in defi/stablecoin/Algorithmic.sol model a mint/burn arbitrage between a stable and a share token, then test/defi/DeathSpiral.t.sol simulating a depeg that hyperinflates the share token. Done when: the simulation reproduces the reflexive spiral — a demand shock forces share-token supply to explode and the peg to break, illustrating why the model is fragile.

requirements.purpose: Trace the original market module's burn-offer and mint-ask state transition rather than relying on a secondary collapse narrative

proposedTopics.title: Sky / USDS (MakerDAO evolution)
proposedTopics.description: Sky's USDS is a distinct upgradeable ERC-20 connected to Maker/Sky's internal accounting through UsdsJoin. The permissionless DaiUsds convenience contract converts DAI and USDS in either direction at 1:1 by routing through DaiJoin and UsdsJoin; it does not establish that the two token addresses or implementation surfaces are interchangeable. The canonical USDS token repository documents permit, EIP-1271 signatures, and UUPS upgradeability, but no account-freeze function.

proposedTopics.title: Lido stETH & wstETH
proposedTopics.description: Lido's stETH is share-accounted and normally rebases when oracle reports update pooled ether; balances can increase or decrease with rewards and penalties. wstETH is the non-rebasing wrapper: its token balance changes only on transfer, mint, or burn, while its stETH-denominated value follows the stETH-per-wstETH rate. Integrations that cannot safely account for rebases use wstETH or operate directly in stETH shares.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in defi/staking/WstEth.sol implement a wrap/unwrap around a mock rebasing stETH, where wstETH balance is constant and value grows via the exchange rate; test/defi/WstEth.t.sol rebases the underlying. proposedTopics.title: EigenLayer restaking
proposedTopics.description: EigenLayer restaking lets native ETH or supported tokens be delegated to operators that opt into additional validation services. Delegated stake can earn service rewards, but stake allocated to an operator's service obligations can be slashed for attributable faults under those obligations. The delegation relationship therefore adds operator and service-specific risk beyond ordinary Ethereum staking.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in defi/staking/Restaking.sol model a strategy where a staker delegates to an operator, an AVS registers a slashing condition, and a proven fault slashes the operator's delegated stake; test/defi/Restaking.t.sol. Done when: delegated stake earns AVS rewards, a proven fault slashes the correct amount from the operator's restakers, and an undelegated staker is unaffected.

proposedTopics.title: Perpetual funding rate (mark vs index)
proposedTopics.description: A perpetual future has no expiry, so periodic peer-to-peer funding helps keep its traded price near an external spot index. Hyperliquid normalizes an impact-bid/ask premium by its spot oracle, averages samples, adds a clamped interest adjustment, caps the hourly rate, and settles against oracle-priced position notional. Positive funding makes longs pay shorts; negative funding reverses the direction.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in defi/perps/Funding.sol implement Hyperliquid's averaged premium-index formula, clamped interest adjustment, hourly cap, and oracle-notional settlement; test/defi/Funding.t.sol. Done when: an impact bid above the oracle produces positive funding and longs pay shorts, an impact ask below the oracle reverses the direction, the clamp and cap bind at their boundaries, and payment uses size * oraclePrice rather than mark price.

proposedTopics.title: GMX GM pools
proposedTopics.description: A GMX GM market has an index price feed plus long and short backing tokens; the index token need not be held by the pool. GM liquidity providers earn protocol fees and are exposed as the counterparty to trader PnL. Orders use oracle mark prices rather than a reserve curve, but GMX separately applies configured price impact based on market imbalance. Two-phase execution commits orders before oracle prices are supplied, reducing front-running risk.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in defi/perps/GmPool.sol model a GM pool where LP value moves inversely to net trader PnL and trades price off an injected oracle (not an AMM curve); test/defi/GmPool.t.sol. Done when: a profitable trader's gain reduces LP pool value by the same amount, and trade execution uses the oracle price rather than pool reserves.

proposedTopics.title: ERC-4626 yield vault mechanics
proposedTopics.description: ERC-4626 standardizes shares over one ERC-20 asset. convertToShares and convertToAssets must round down; state-changing preview paths use opposing vault-favorable directions—deposit/redeem output rounds down, while mint/withdraw required input rounds up. Yield can raise assets per share without rebasing shares. A virtual-asset/share offset can make first-depositor donation attacks unprofitable, but it is an implementation defense rather than a requirement of EIP-4626 itself.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: implement defi/vault/YieldVault4626.sol from scratch (deposit/mint/withdraw/redeem + convertTo* with vault-favorable rounding and a virtual-offset), simulating yield by donating asset over time; test/defi/YieldVault4626.t.sol. Done when: a fuzz test proves totalAssets/totalSupply never lets a redeemer extract more than deposited-plus-yield, rounding always favors the vault, and the first-depositor inflation attack fails.

requirements.purpose: Map deposit, mint, withdraw, redeem, convert, and preview methods to their normative rounding directions

proposedTopics.title: Aave flash loans
proposedTopics.description: Aave flashLoan and flashLoanSimple transfer liquidity and invoke executeOperation on a receiver inside one transaction. For the simple path, the receiver must approve the pool to pull principal plus the pool's configured premium after the callback; failure reverts the transaction. The premium is governance-configurable and must be read from the pool rather than hard-coded. The multi-asset path has additional modes, including opening debt when authorized.

Done when: exact configured repayment succeeds, under-repayment reverts the entire transaction with pool and receiver balances restored, and changing the mock premium requires no borrower code change.

proposedTopics.title: Flash-loan use cases (arb, liquidation, collateral swap)
proposedTopics.description: A flash loan supplies capital for one atomic transaction, enabling cross-venue arbitrage, liquidations, and collateral or debt swaps without pre-funding the borrowed principal. It is bounded by available pool liquidity, not unbounded. Every path must leave enough of the repayment asset for principal plus premium before the callback ends or revert. The same composability can amplify oracle-manipulation attacks, so consumers must secure pricing rather than assume flash liquidity can be blocked.

Done when: the liquidation nets a profit atomically without pre-funding the borrowed principal, and if the seized collateral can't cover loan+premium the whole transaction reverts.

proposedPrompts.promptText: How does an aToken's balance grow without any transfer, and how is that implemented?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: An aToken is a scaled-balance token: your stored scaledBalance is fixed at deposit, but balanceOf = scaledBalance * liquidityIndex / RAY, and the liquidity index rises continuously with accrued interest — so balanceOf increases over time with no transfer. Debt uses the same trick with a borrow index. Pitfall: because the balance rebases, integrating aTokens like a static ERC-20 (caching a balance, or treating it as fee-on-transfer-free) silently mis-accounts interest.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write Aave's health-factor formula and state exactly when a position becomes liquidatable.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: HF = sum(collateral_i * liquidationThreshold_i) / totalDebt, all valued in one base currency; the position is liquidatable the moment HF < 1. Borrowing is capped at the lower max-LTV, and the liquidation threshold sits above LTV to leave a buffer. A liquidator repays up to the close factor of the debt and seizes collateral plus a liquidation bonus. Pitfall: use the LIQUIDATION THRESHOLD, not the LTV, in the HF numerator — mixing them up either blocks valid liquidations or lets bad debt accrue.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Implement computeHealthFactor for a single collateral/debt pair (18-decimal base).
proposedPrompts.answerHint: function healthFactor(uint collUsd, uint liqThresholdBps, uint debtUsd) pure returns (uint) { if (debtUsd == 0) return type(uint).max; uint weighted = Math.mulDiv(collUsd, liqThresholdBps, 10_000); return Math.mulDiv(weighted, 1e18, debtUsd); } // HF < 1e18 means liquidatable

proposedPrompts.promptText: How did Aave v3.7 replace legacy isolation mode with isolated e-mode?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: E-mode applies governance-configured category LTV, liquidation, and borrowing permissions. In v3.7 an isolated e-mode lets only category collateral contribute LTV, blocks entry while outside collateral is enabled, and prevents enabling outside collateral after entry. It replaces the legacy isolated-collateral mechanism with approved debt assets and a debt ceiling, which v3.7 removes. Pitfall: rollout and category parameters are market configuration, and correlation assumptions can fail.

proposedPrompts.promptText: How does Compound V3 (Comet) differ structurally from a pooled Aave-style market?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Comet has a SINGLE borrowable base asset per deployment (e.g. USDC): you earn/borrow only the base asset, and every other supported asset is collateral ONLY — it backs your borrow, earns no supply interest, and cannot itself be borrowed. This isolates each market's risk to one base asset and its curated collateral, versus Aave's shared multi-asset pool. Pitfall: don't expect to earn yield on collateral in Comet — supplying a collateral asset is not the same as supplying the base asset.

proposedPrompts.promptText: How does an overcollateralized CDP mint a stablecoin and keep it near $1?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Lock collateral worth more than the debt and mint the coin up to a minimum collateralization ratio (e.g. 150% -> max ~66% of collateral value as debt); burn the coin to unlock collateral. The peg holds via overcollateralization plus arbitrage: below $1 the coin is cheap to buy and repay debt at par (worth $1 of collateral release), above $1 it's profitable to mint and sell. Pitfall: the whole system's solvency rides on the collateral PRICE FEED — a manipulated or stale oracle either mis-mints or hides insolvent vaults.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Cyfrin Updraft (Advanced Foundry) — build the DecentralizedStableCoin + DSCEngine and pass the invariant suite.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Implement an ERC-20 stablecoin plus an engine that deposits collateral, mints DSC bounded by a health factor derived from a Chainlink feed, redeems, and liquidates undercollateralized positions with a bonus; write an invariant test asserting protocol collateral value always exceeds total DSC supply. It is the canonical from-scratch CDP exercise.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Define a CDP's collateralization ratio and explain why the oracle is its most critical dependency.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Ratio = collateralValueUSD / debtValueUSD; below the protocol's liquidation ratio a keeper liquidates — repaying debt from collateral and taking a penalty/bonus. Both values come from an oracle, so a stale or manipulated price can trigger unfair liquidations (price reads too low) or hide insolvent vaults (price reads too high), directly threatening the peg and solvency. Pitfall: liquidations must stay incentive-compatible even in a gas spike / price crash, or nobody liquidates and the protocol accrues bad debt.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Why are seigniorage-style algorithmic stablecoins structurally fragile, using UST/LUNA as the example?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Terra Classic's market module burned the offered native coin and minted the requested coin at oracle exchange rates. When stablecoin exits require minting a volatile sister asset, falling sister-asset price means each redemption requires more issuance, which can further weaken price and redemption capacity. After the May 2022 collapse, market-module swaps were disabled on Terra Classic and the new Terra chain launched without native stablecoins or that module. Pitfall: mint/burn convertibility is not collateral; it depends on demand for the asset being issued.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What is the relationship between DAI and USDS after MakerDAO's rebrand to Sky?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: USDS is a distinct upgradeable ERC-20. The permissionless DaiUsds convenience contract converts DAI and USDS both ways at 1:1 by using DaiJoin and UsdsJoin; it does not make their token addresses or implementation surfaces identical. The canonical USDS repository documents permit, EIP-1271 signatures, and UUPS upgradeability, but no account-freeze function. Pitfall: parity through a converter is not ERC-20 identity—integrations must configure each address and its actual contract behavior.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Why does DeFi prefer wstETH over stETH, given they represent the same staked ETH?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: stETH is share-accounted and normally rebases when Lido's oracle report changes pooled ether; balances can rise with rewards or fall with penalties. wstETH represents those shares with a non-rebasing ERC-20 balance, while stETH-per-wstETH changes. That is safer for systems that cannot account for balance changes without transfers. Pitfall: neither token is mechanically fixed at 1 ETH—use the current share/wrapper rate and account for rounding.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What does EigenLayer restaking add on top of Ethereum staking, and what is the new risk?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Restaking reuses staked ETH/LSTs to opt into securing additional services (AVSs); stakers delegate to operators who run AVS software and earn extra rewards, extending Ethereum's pooled crypto-economic security to oracles/bridges/DA layers. The new risk is ADDITIONAL, AVS-specific slashing on top of Ethereum's — each AVS defines its own fault conditions. Pitfall: stacking many AVSs multiplies slashing surface and can create correlated-failure risk if operators over-commit the same stake across risky services.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write a scaled-balance balanceOf so an aToken accrues interest without transfers.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: function balanceOf(address u) public view returns (uint) { return scaledBalance[u].rayMulFloor(liquidityIndex()); } // mint stores amount.rayDivFloor(index); burn/transfer convert assets to scaled balances with ceil rounding

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write Hyperliquid's funding-rate and payment kernel from an averaged premium index.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: int adjustment = clamp(interestRate8hWad - averagePremiumWad, -5e14, 5e14); int rate8hWad = averagePremiumWad + adjustment; int hourlyRateWad = clamp(rate8hWad / 8, -4e16, 4e16); int payment = int(positionSize) * int(oraclePrice) / 1e18 * hourlyRateWad / 1e18; // positive: long pays short; use oracle notional

proposedPrompts.promptText: What is the funding rate on a perpetual future, and which direction does it push?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: A periodic peer-to-peer payment between longs and shorts that helps tether the perp to spot. On Hyperliquid, impact bid/ask prices form a premium normalized by the spot oracle; sampled premiums are averaged, adjusted by a clamped interest term, and capped. Positive funding makes LONGS pay SHORTS; negative funding reverses it. Payment uses position size * oracle price * funding rate, not mark-price notional. Pitfall: funding is not a protocol fee, and weak oracle or impact-price inputs can distort it.

proposedPrompts.promptText: In a GMX V2 GM pool, what side do liquidity providers take, and how are trades priced?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: A GM market holds long and short backing tokens and references an index price feed; it need not hold the index token. LPs earn fees and are counterparty to aggregate trader PnL, so trader profit reduces pool value. Orders use oracle mark prices instead of a reserve curve, but configured price impact is applied separately from slippage based on imbalance. Two-phase execution commits the order before oracle prices arrive. Pitfall: GM liquidity is market-specific counterparty and token exposure, not risk-free yield.

proposedPrompts.promptText: How does Hyperliquid's liquidity model differ from an AMM, and what backstops it?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: HyperCore runs fully on-chain order books on Hyperliquid's purpose-built L1; resting orders match by price-time priority rather than a bonding curve. Liquidations first submit market orders to that book. If a position remains deeply below maintenance margin, it can be transferred to the liquidator vault, a component strategy of HLP. Pitfall: HLP is not the matching rule or sole source of ordinary liquidity—the public order book matches all resting orders.

proposedPrompts.promptText: State the ERC-4626 share/asset conversion and the two rounding rules that keep the vault solvent.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Ignoring virtual terms, convertToShares = assets*totalSupply/totalAssets and convertToAssets is the inverse; both convert functions must round down. For state-changing previews, deposit/redeem outputs round down while mint/withdraw required inputs round up. A virtual asset plus virtual shares (optionally with a decimal offset) can make donation attacks unprofitable. Pitfall: that defense is implementation-specific, and totalAssets semantics come from the vault—not an assumption that raw balanceOf is always correct.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write ERC-4626 convertToShares with vault-favorable (round-down) behavior and virtual offset.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: function convertToShares(uint assets) view returns (uint) { return Math.mulDiv(assets, totalSupply() + 10 ** _decimalsOffset(), totalAssets() + 1, Math.Rounding.Floor); } // virtual asset + virtual shares; convertToShares rounds down

proposedPrompts.promptText: What makes an Aave flash loan safe despite being uncollateralized, and how is repayment enforced?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Atomicity: the pool transfers funds and calls executeOperation; after the callback, flashLoanSimple pulls principal plus the configured premium. If approval or balance is insufficient, the entire transaction reverts. The premium is governance-configurable, so receiver logic must use the callback value or query current pool configuration rather than hard-code 0.05%. Pitfall: flashLoan has multiple assets and can open authorized debt modes, while flashLoanSimple is the repay-with-premium path.

proposedPrompts.topicTitle: Flash-loan use cases (arb, liquidation, collateral swap)
proposedPrompts.promptText: Name three legitimate flash-loan strategies and the constraint they all share.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Cross-venue arbitrage, liquidations, and collateral swaps or debt refinancing. Each path must end the callback with enough of the repayment asset for principal plus premium, within available pool liquidity, or the transaction reverts. The principal need not be pre-funded, but gas, execution risk, slippage limits, and any shortfall still matter. Pitfall: flash liquidity can amplify oracle manipulation, so consumers must harden price sources rather than assume the primitive can be blocked.

proposedPrompts.topicTitle: Flash-loan use cases (arb, liquidation, collateral swap)
proposedPrompts.promptText: Damn Vulnerable DeFi — Naive Receiver: drain a flash-loan receiver that pays the fee on every call.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: The receiver pays a fixed fee for any flash loan and doesn't check who initiated it, so anyone can force it to take repeated (even zero-value) loans until its balance is bled out in fees to the pool. The lesson: a flash-loan receiver must authenticate the initiator and validate loan parameters, not blindly pay on callback.
